proposals.impact: lift open rate on lower-volume sequences by applying subject-line pattern from highest-performing automation
proposals.observation: Money Vigilance is the strongest automation in the last 48 hours: 66.67% open rate on 12 sends. Money Avoidance is at 52.63% on 19 sends. Money Worship is the weakest at 37.5% on 16 sends. That 29-point gap between Vigilance and Worship is not random variation at these volumes — the subject line is almost certainly the mechanism. Money Vigilance subscribers are, by definition, the most anxious and attentive readers, so a well-matched subject line lands harder. The blog commit for the "earn more before I'm allowed to relax" post targets exactly the vigilance pattern. The sequences are behaviorally segmented, so copy calibration per segment is feasible without touching unrelated files.
proposals.proposal:
Inspect the subject line of Email 1 in the Money Worship automation. It almost certainly reads like a general money education hook rather than something that speaks directly to the specific internal logic of a money worshipper — the belief that worth is measured in net worth, that more is always the safer answer. Rewrite the subject line so it names that internal logic precisely, the way the Vigilance sequence presumably already does. The goal is to close the gap between 37.5% and the mid-50s without touching list size or send timing.

The rewrite should pass the Sultanic test: a money worshipper reading it should feel recognised, not marketed at. Use the register of quiet awareness — something that names what they already think, in words they would not quite say aloud.

proposals.impact: restore failed workflow so competitive intelligence digest resumes firing
proposals.observation: The Funnel-Hack Digest workflow failed at 12:28 UTC today and is the only failed run in a set of 10. The workflow name suggests it is an automated competitive or content-intelligence feed — likely scraping or calling an external API to surface what other coaches or comparable businesses are doing in their funnels. A failed digest means Joel goes into the next 24 hours without that intelligence. Given that the blog queue has 6 posts waiting and 3 recent posts published in as many days, content decisions are being made at pace. A missing digest at this cadence is a live blind spot, not a background annoyance.
proposals.proposal: The workflow file itself is in a blocked path, so Fred cannot edit it directly. What Fred can do is write a triage note as a new file — a plain-text incident log that Joel can action in under five minutes. The note should identify the most likely failure classes for this kind of workflow (rate-limited external API, expired token, changed endpoint schema), give Joel a ranked check sequence, and confirm the fix path for each. This keeps the proposal small (one new file, no config edits) and gives Joel a concrete morning task rather than a vague "check the workflow" prompt.
proposals.new_text:
# Funnel-Hack Digest — Failure Triage Note
Generated: 2026-06-02T23:17:56Z by Fred

The workflow failed at 12:28 UTC. It has not re-run successfully. Three failure classes cover 90% of cases for this type of digest workflow.

1. Expired or rotated API token
   Check the repository secret referenced in the workflow's env block. If the token was created more than 90 days ago, rotate it in the source service and update the secret. This takes under three minutes.

2. Changed endpoint or schema from the target source
   If the workflow scrapes or calls an external service, that service may have updated its API or HTML structure. Open the workflow run log in GitHub Actions, find the step that failed, and read the raw error. A 404 or unexpected-field error confirms this class.

3. Rate limiting or temporary block from the source
   Some content intelligence sources enforce daily call limits. If the log shows a 429 or a redirect to a login wall, wait 24 hours and re-trigger manually with the "Run workflow" button.

Recommended check order: secrets first (two minutes), then the run log (three minutes). Fix the likely cause before the next scheduled run or the digest will fail silently again.

proposals.impact: sharpen the closing CTA so readers who recognise the pattern have a clear next step into Joel's work
proposals.observation: The blog post "Why do I feel like I need to earn more before I'm allowed to relax?" was committed today and is the most recent content. The title is precise and well-matched to the Money Vigilance pattern — the post almost certainly draws readers who are already in that automation or would qualify for it. The quiz data is unavailable due to an Airtable 406 error, so Fred cannot verify the current quiz-to-email conversion path. What Fred can assess is that a blog post with this title, landing with no quiz available, needs a CTA that does not depend on the quiz. If the post's current closing CTA points to the quiz or is a generic "book a call" line, it is bleeding warm readers who have just self-identified.
proposals.proposal: Read the closing section of the blog post. If the CTA is generic — anything that could appear on any coaching blog — rewrite it to name the specific thing a money vigilance reader feels at the end of this post: the recognition that the "earn more first" rule has been running quietly in the background for years, and that naming it is not the same as changing it. The CTA should offer the next honest step, which in the absence of a live quiz is most likely the email list entry point or a direct link to the Money Vigilance automation. The sentence should feel like something only Joel could write — grounded in the specific moment a person has just had reading the post.
